# Page 2^page=2
©Idaho State University, 2021 SCOPE AND CONTENT NOTE The James Aho Collection is comprised of a variety of materials documenting right-wing extremism in Idaho and the Pacific Northwest. Materials consist of printed matter, recordings, and ephemera including, newspapers, programs, newsletters, brochures, advertisements, correspondence, research papers, legal proceedings, recorded sermons, and interviews. The bulk of the collection consists of newsletters from various churches and organizations promoting their beliefs, and, recorded sermons on cassette tapes that cover a variety of topics. ARRANGEMENT: The Collection is arranged by material type in eight (8) series and fifteen (15) subseries: I. Newsletters; II. Articles; III. Booklets, Brochures, Pamphlets, Papers; IV. Correspondence; V. Legal; VI. Newspapers; VII. Recordings; VIII. Research Notes. SERIES I: Newsletters Subseries 1: Scriptures for America Subseries 2: The Dragon Slayer Subseries 3: The Page Subseries 4: The American Mercury Subseries 5: Destiny Magazine Subseries 6: Aryan Nations Subseries 7: The Covenant Message Subseries 8: Civil Liberties Review Subseries 9: Liberty Lobby Subseries 10: Miscellaneous SERIES II: Articles Subseries 1: Newspaper Articles Subseries 2: Magazine Articles Subseries 3: Research Articles SERIES III: Ephemera SERIES IV: Correspondence SERIES V: Legal SERIES VI: Newspapers

# Page 4^page=4
©Idaho State University, 2021 BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE James Aho was born in 1942 in Aberdeen, Washington. During the 1950s his family moved from Aberdeen to Shelton, Washington, where he graduated from Reed High School in 1961. Aho continued his education at the University of Washington, where he received a BA in Sociology in 1965; and a MA and Ph.D. in Sociology from Washington State University in 1968 and 1971, respectively. Dr. Aho began teaching at Idaho State University in 1969 as a Sociology Instructor, with promotions to Assistant Professor in 1971 and to full Professor in 1982. In 1985, he began researching religiously-motivated hate groups located in the Pacific Northwest, a project that would last ten years. He retired as Professor of Sociology from Idaho State University in January 2009, after teaching over forty years. During his time at ISU he authored many books, articles, reports, and reviews, and was honored as both a Distinguished Researcher and as a Distinguished Teacher. His research covered a vast area, from religion and violence and right-wing extremism, to the sociology of modern accounting and the sociology of the body.
